December 31 Year-End vs a Non-Calendar Year-End

What the fiscal year-end date changes about a nil T2, what it does not, and why December 31 is a convention rather than a rule.

Start Nil T2 Filing NOWSee Every Due Date

Quick Answer

Both are the same return at the same price. The year-end sets the deadline and almost nothing else. A December 31 year-end makes the T2 due the following June 30; any other year-end makes it due six months after that date. December 31 is a convention rather than a rule, nothing assigns a year-end at incorporation, and what fixes it is the first T2 return filed. Either way the filing is $300.00 plus HST per tax year, carries the same schedules and is transmitted the same way.

Nil T2 filing in Canada › Nil T2 filing price › December 31 Year-End vs a Non-Calendar Year-End

Written and reviewed by Sharad Gondaliya, CPA (Ontario), CPA Ontario Membership 61040184.

Last reviewed: November 4, 2026

The Date Moves the Deadline, Not the Return

A quiet year is the same piece of work whenever it ends. The year-end decides when the return is due and when the records are wanted, and that is the whole of its effect on a nil filing. It does not change which schedules attach, who signs, how the return is transmitted or what it costs.

December 31 is worth no more and no less than any other date. It is common because it lines up with the calendar most people already keep, not because anything in the rules prefers it, and a corporation that picked August 31 is in exactly the same position six months after August 31.

This comparison sets two of our own filing routes against each other and names no other provider. Where a comparison on this site does name one, it states that provider’s published prices and published features only.

Nothing Assigns You a Year-End

The date is a decision rather than a default:

  • A corporation picks its own fiscal year-end. There is no default and nothing is allocated at incorporation.
  • The articles of incorporation do not set it either. What sets it is the first T2 return filed.
  • A first tax year runs from the date of incorporation to the chosen year-end and may not exceed 53 weeks, which is 371 days counting the day of incorporation.
  • Once the first return is filed the date is on the record and it recurs annually.
  • Changing it afterwards needs the written approval of the Canada Revenue Agency.
  • A short year does not get an early deadline. The six months are counted from the day that short year ends.

A year-end that does not match the one on the record gets the transmission rejected. Where no return has ever been filed the date is still unsettled, and the first return filed is what settles it.

A corporation incorporated in September that picked August 31

Its first tax year runs from the September incorporation date to the following August 31, which is inside the 53-week limit, so the date is available. That first return is due the following February 28 or 29, six months after August 31, and every year after it runs on the same cycle. Nothing about the quiet year is different from a December 31 corporation: the same schedules where anything sits on the books, the same Form T183CORP, and $300.00 plus HST per tax year. The figures here illustrate how the rules apply and are not drawn from a client file.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does the year-end change what a nil return costs?

No. The fee is $300.00 plus HST per tax year on any year-end. The date moves the deadline, not the price.

Is December 31 the default year-end?

No. December 31 is a convention rather than a rule. Nothing is allocated at incorporation and the articles of incorporation do not set a date either.

Then what sets my year-end?

The first T2 return filed. From then on the date is on the record and it recurs annually.

When is the return due on a December 31 year-end?

June 30 the following year, which is simply the six-month rule applied to December 31.

How do I work out the date on another year-end?

Count six months to the same day number in the later month. An August 31 year-end falls on the last day of February, because there is no thirty-first of February.

Can I still pick my year-end?

Only until the first return is filed. If no return has ever been filed the date is still unsettled, and the first one filed settles it.

How long can the first tax year be?

Up to 53 weeks, which is 371 days counting the day of incorporation. A year-end chosen further out than that is not available, so the first year has to end earlier.

Can I change the year-end later?

Changing it needs the written approval of the Canada Revenue Agency. It is not something a corporation does by filing on a different date.

Does a short year get an earlier deadline?

No. The six months are counted from the day the short year ends, exactly as they are for a full one.

What happens if I file on the wrong year-end?

A year-end that does not match the one on the record gets the transmission rejected, which is one of the more common reasons a return does not go through first time.

Is a December 31 year-end simpler to keep?

It lines up with the calendar most people already keep, so the records are wanted alongside everything else dated December 31. That is convenience, not a rule, and it changes nothing about the return.

Do the schedules depend on the year-end?

No. The schedules follow what sits on the corporation’s books, not the date the year ended.

Does a non-calendar year-end make a nil return harder to file?

No. The work is the same and the route is the same. Only the dates differ.

Which year-end should a new corporation pick?

That is a decision for the corporation and its own circumstances. What matters here is that the choice is made before the first return goes in, and that it sits inside the 53-week limit.

Which tool should I run first?

The nil T2 deadline calculator, which dates the return from any year-end you give it.
